credit: Plates: illuminations and drawings from the Wenceslas Bible (Vienna), Ulrich Richental's chronicle (Konstanz, Rosgartenmuseum), the Martinice Bible, a fifteenth-century Prague manuscript with Jerome's shield of faith and the Jena Codex (Prague), and a Poggio manuscript from the library of Urbino (Vatican); a notarial instrument of 1414 (Prague); and a wood engraving from Zap's Česko-moravská kronika (1868). Public-domain reproductions via Wikimedia Commons, resized for this site.
lede: The king, the council, the condemned man and the captain, as painters of the fifteenth century saw them. Each plate names its source; the caption points to the passage it belongs with. The burning itself is not shown.

plates.caption: The king enthroned with sword and orb, in an initial of the German Bible made for him in Prague in the 1390s. It was Wenceslas who gave the Bohemian nation three votes at the university (KH Mandate [1]) and who protected Hus until 1412; his death in August 1419 left the crown to his brother Sigismund.
plates.source: Wenceslas Bible, Vienna, Österreichische Nationalbibliothek, Cod. 2759–2764, c. 1389–1400 (detail); via Wikimedia Commons.

plates.titel: A notarial instrument in the Carolinum
plates.caption: Wikimedia Commons labels this sealed sheet 'Decree of Kutná Hora'. Its opening lines date it to September of the year 1414 (indiction seven) in the Collegium Carolinum, and Master Jan Hus of Husinec is named a few lines down: it is a notarial instrument drawn up at the university, not the king's letter of 1409, whose text Palacký took from the university's statute book (KH Mandate [1]). It shows the form in which the university's business was certified and kept.
plates.source: Prague, 1414, parchment with pendant seal; image from the Library of the Czech Academy of Sciences, via Wikimedia Commons (public domain).

plates.titel: A session of the council in the cathedral
plates.caption: The pope (in the council's first months, John XXIII), standing at the altar, with cardinals and bishops on the benches of Constance cathedral and the common people behind the barrier. The council's general sessions were held here; here Haec sancta was passed (Decr. Haec [1]) and Hus was sentenced (Decr. Sentence [1]).
plates.source: Ulrich Richental, Chronicle of the Council of Constance, Konstanz, Rosgartenmuseum, Hs. 1, fol. 12v, c. 1460–1465; via Wikimedia Commons.

plates.titel: The degradation and the way out of the city
plates.caption: Above, bishops strip Hus of his priestly vestments; the inscription reads 'de degradacione Husso'. Below, wearing the paper crown painted with devils, he is led out of Constance among armed men. The chronicle's next picture shows the burning, which this site does not reproduce. Mladoňovice tells the degradation (Mlad. Sentence [2]); Richental the handing over (Richental [2]).
plates.source: Ulrich Richental, Chronicle of the Council of Constance, Konstanz, Rosgartenmuseum, Hs. 1, fol. 57v, c. 1460–1465; via Wikimedia Commons.

plates.caption: A nineteenth-century picture of 2 September 1415: lords at a table in a Gothic hall hang their seals on the letter of complaint. Its Czech caption reads 'The lords at the diet hang their seals on the letter of complaint over the burning of Hus, 1415'. It is how the national history of the 1860s saw the protest: as the nobility of the land standing together. The letter itself went to Constance in eight copies under 452 seals (Protest [3]).
plates.source: Wood engraving after Antonín König, in K. V. Zap, Česko-moravská kronika (Prague: Kober, 1868), p. 700; via Wikimedia Commons (public domain).

plates.caption: The old diagram of the Trinity, the 'shield of faith', in the version associated with Jerome of Prague. The verse at the top reads 'Snow, ice, rain: three names, yet one thing; so God is threefold, yet one'. Each of the four fields lists five matching terms: Father, ice, memory, eagle, Augustine; Son, rain, reason, lion, Jerome; Spirit, snow, will, calf, Ambrose; and in the middle God, water, the rational soul, animal, man. It is the philosophical realism, the reality of universals, that Jerome had defended in the universities of Europe, and that his accusers held against him.
plates.source: Prague, National Library of the Czech Republic, MS V E 28, fol. 130r, fifteenth century; via Wikimedia Commons (public domain).

plates.caption: The Florentine humanist, grey-haired, with an open book, in the initial of a manuscript of his dialogue On the Variety of Fortune from the ducal library of Urbino. At Constance in 1416 he was a papal secretary without a pope, hunting manuscripts in the monasteries round the lake, and he wrote to Leonardo Bruni that he had never heard anyone come nearer to the eloquence of the ancients than Jerome (Poggio [1]).
plates.source: Vatican Library, Urb. lat. 224, fifteenth century (detail); via Wikimedia Commons (public domain).

plates.caption: In the initial I of Genesis, beside the days of creation, Hus stands in the fire with the heretic's paper crown; at the left a master in a dark gown holds a book. The Bible was made in Bohemia around 1430, fifteen years after the death; it has been suggested that the master is Peter of Mladoňovice, who may have ordered the manuscript. Within a generation Hus had become a martyr painted into scripture.
plates.source: Martinice Bible, Prague, Library of the Czech Academy of Sciences, fol. 11v, c. 1430; via Wikimedia Commons.

plates.caption: Jan Žižka, blind, on a white horse, with the chalice on the banner a mace in his hand, and his men behind him with halberds and a war hammer; the scroll calls him 'Žižka, our faithful brother'. Painted some eighty years after his death in 1424, for the Utraquist community that kept his memory.
plates.source: Jena Codex (Antithesis Christi et Antichristi), Prague, National Museum Library, c. 1490–1510, attributed to Janíček Zmilelý of Písek; via Wikimedia Commons.
